title: Afghanistan’s girls can attend primary school. Who will teach the next class?
subtitle: A UN assessment found that only one in four fourth-graders met the third-grade standard in maths. As the number of women teachers falls, girls who hope to join them cannot study beyond sixth grade.

paragraphs.text: In Herat, primary teacher Zarghuna Afghan had her third-graders count seeds together. She ended the lesson the way she usually did, with a story and no homework. Afghan had returned to education after an early marriage and earned a university degree. For the girls in her class at Asem Primary School, the Taliban’s ban on education beyond sixth grade closes the route their teacher took.

A report released on 4 November by UNESCO and UNICEF shows what is at stake well before girls reach that cutoff. In a national assessment of more than 55,000 pupils across Afghanistan’s 34 provinces, fewer than half of fourth-graders met the previous year’s language standard. Only one in four met the third-grade standard in maths. The assessment describes children who made it into a classroom; it cannot tell us how children outside school would have scored.

Afghan described her lesson to UNICEF in March. She was one of 30 teachers in Herat taking part in a British-funded pilot that offered extra classes during school holidays. She said teaching through play had changed how she ran her classroom: children joined in more readily and she felt less need to discipline them. Her account shows what training allowed one teacher to try. It does not establish how much the programme raised test scores.

The harder question for schools is who will be there to teach when women like Afghan retire. UNICEF found that the number of women teaching in basic education fell from nearly 73,000 in 2022 to about 66,000 in 2024. Teaching is still one of the occupations open to women. But a girl who wants to enter it cannot finish secondary school in Afghanistan, and women are barred from its universities. UNICEF estimated in April that the country could lose up to 20,000 women teachers by 2030 if the restrictions persist. That is a projection, separate from the decline already recorded.

Families continue to find places for their children to learn. In October, roughly 162,000 learners attended 5,300 community-run classes; girls accounted for 64 per cent of enrolments. These classes can bring lessons within reach where a school is inaccessible. Their enrolment figures cover learners of different ages and do not show that teenage girls have regained a place in secondary school. UNESCO and UNICEF estimate that more than 2.6 million girls have been denied that opportunity since 2021.

The two agencies are asking for investment in teachers and classroom materials as well as the restoration of girls’ right to study. The distinction matters in Herat. A holiday class gives a girl time to practise her sums and a teacher the freedom to explain them another way. Whether that girl can stay in school long enough to become the teacher herself is a decision only the authorities can change.
